title: Layer-Hybridized Wigner Crystals in MoSe2/WS2 Moiré Superlattice
authors: Tianyi Ouyang, Yuze Meng, Li Yan, Yuxuan Chen, Shuai Zhang, Xinyue Chen, Melike Erdi, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, Seth Ariel Tongay, Benjamin Hunt, Ming Xie, Yong-Tao Cui, Su-Fei Shi
abstract: Transition metal dichalcogenide moiré heterobilayers with type-II band alignment provide a versatile platform for layer-polarized generalized Wigner crystals, in which strong Coulomb interactions drive charge ordering at fractional lattice fillings. With a finite interlayer band offset, an out-of-plane electric field can tune layer-resolved moiré bands through resonance and enable controllable interlayer hybridization. Although hybridized Mott insulators have been previously demonstrated, whether fractional charge-ordered states can survive such hybridization remains elusive. Here we drive an H-stacked MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer through a type-I-to-type-II band-alignment transition and realize layer-hybridized Mott insulator and generalized Wigner crystals. For fillings below one electron per moiré cell, tunneling delocalizes electrons and modifies Wigner crystallization. However, above one electron per cell, Coulomb repulsion overcomes tunneling and favors layer-separated occupation, stabilizing stronger charge-ordered states. These results establish electrically tunable hybridized moiré heterobilayers as a powerful platform for engineering correlated charge order and exploring fractional Chern phases and emergent magnetism.
summary: This work demonstrates that MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayers can act as tunable platforms for engineering correlated electronic states like Mott insulators and Wigner crystals. By applying an out-of-plane electric field, researchers control the interlayer hybridization, showing that charge ordering is stabilized differently depending on whether the electron density is below or above one per moiré cell.
main_problem: The study investigates whether fractional charge-ordered states, such as Generalized Wigner Crystals (GWC), can survive when interlayer hybridization is induced in moiré heterobilayers.
main_result: The system exhibits layer-hybridized Mott insulators and GWCs whose stability depends strongly on the electron filling factor ($n$); specifically, strong correlation is favored at fillings above one electron per moiré cell due to Coulomb repulsion overcoming tunneling.
method: The research combines optical characterization (reflectance contrast spectroscopy using Rydberg excitons) with magneto-optical measurements (Magnetic Circular Dichroism, MCD) across varying out-of-plane electric fields.
model_or_system: The physical system is an H-stacked MoSe2/WS2 moiré heterobilayer. The analysis uses concepts of layer-polarized generalized Wigner crystals and Mott insulators, tunable via an external electric field that controls the band alignment between the two semiconducting layers.
key_observables: MCD spectra (sensitive to magnetism), doping-dependent reflectance contrast spectroscopy, hybridization energy ($t$), and charge ordering signatures at fractional fillings.
important_parameters: Filling factor ($n$) relative to unity, out-of-plane electric field strength ($	ext{V/nm}$), and the resulting band alignment regime (Type-I vs. Type-II).
main_assumptions: The system can be modeled by considering the competition between interlayer tunneling (kinetic energy) and on-site Coulomb repulsion, which dictates charge localization.
figures_summary: Figures detail doping-dependent reflectance contrast spectra showing Hubbard band splitting under varying electric fields, alongside MCD measurements confirming magnetic signatures across different hybridization regimes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically maps the electronic state evolution by first characterizing the moiré superlattice structure and then using electric field tuning to transition between different band alignments (Type-I $	o$ Type-II), observing changes in correlated insulating states (Mott/GWC) at varying electron fillings.
why_interesting: The ability to electrically tune correlation strength and charge ordering in a solid-state moiré system provides an accessible platform for studying fundamental many-body physics, analogous to tuning parameters in quantum simulation models.
